title: Postman Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Postman lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Requests and responses
entries.summary: Postman helps inspect HTTP messages. A request asks for work; a response gives a status, headers and sometimes a body.
notes: Reading a sample response does not prove a real service will return it.

entries.name: Read a URL
entries.summary: A URL identifies a destination. Its scheme, host, path and query parts have different roles.

example.code:
https://practice.test/books?title=Moon
Scheme: https
Host: practice.test
Path: /books
Query: title=Moon

notes: Do not send requests to a system you are not authorised to use.

entries.name: GET reads a resource
entries.summary: GET asks for a representation of a resource. It should not be designed as a hidden command to delete or charge something.

example.code:
GET /books/17 HTTP/1.1
Host: practice.test
Accept: application/json

notes: Do not put private secrets in URLs; URLs can appear in logs.

entries.name: POST submits data
entries.summary: POST sends data to a resource for processing. Many APIs use it to create something, according to that API's contract.

example.code:
POST /notes HTTP/1.1
Host: practice.test
Content-Type: application/json

{"text":"Read chapter one"}

notes: Never press Send against a live write endpoint merely to see what happens.

entries.name: PUT PATCH and DELETE
entries.summary: Methods have different intended meanings. PUT commonly replaces a resource representation; PATCH changes part; DELETE requests removal.

example.code:
PUT /notes/3 -> replace the note representation
PATCH /notes/3 -> apply a partial change
DELETE /notes/3 -> request removal

notes: A method name alone does not tell you all the service's business rules.

entries.name: Understand status families
entries.summary: The first status-code digit groups the result. 2xx means success; 4xx indicates a client-side request issue; 5xx indicates a server-side failure.

example.code:
200 OK: successful read
404 Not Found: requested item missing
500 Internal Server Error: server failed

notes: Do not assume every non-200 response is a server crash.

entries.name: Read JSON safely
entries.summary: JSON is a text format for structured data. Object keys and string values use double quotes.
notes: JSON does not allow comments or trailing commas in its standard form.

entries.name: Use variables for repeatable requests
entries.summary: A Postman variable can hold a reusable value such as a base URL. The selected scope controls which value is used.
notes: Do not accidentally switch a harmless practice request to a live write environment.

entries.name: Keep credentials private
entries.summary: Some real APIs need credentials. Use the tool's appropriate local or secret storage and authorised access; do not copy real tokens into examples or public collections.

example.code:
Public collection: request shape and non-secret examples
Private authorised setup: credentials supplied separately

notes: Removing a token from a new export does not revoke a token that was already leaked.

entries.name: Write a response check
entries.summary: A Postman response script can assert facts about the last response. pm is provided by Postman's script environment.
notes: A status check alone does not verify every field in a response body.

entries.name: Check a response field
entries.summary: A body check should use the contract for that request. Read JSON and assert the field you need.
notes: Do not parse every response as JSON without checking the endpoint's contract.

entries.name: Organise and review a collection
entries.summary: A collection groups related requests and examples. Review its target URLs, scripts and exported data before sharing or running it.

example.code:
Collection: Library reads
Requests: find a book, list books
Examples: success and missing-book response
Review: no real credentials or private data

notes: A downloaded collection can contain scripts; inspect it before running.
